config.subtitle: Virology questions sourced from Lippincott's Illustrated Q&A Review of Microbiology & Immunology

questions.stem: An outbreak of Calicivirus occurs in a home for disabled adults. What is an important characteristic of this virus group that influences the occurrence of disease outbreaks and their control and prevention?
choices: Long-term immunity after infection or vaccination
Low infectious dose required for infection
Susceptibility of the virus to chlorine cleaning agents
Susceptibility of the virus to desiccation
Transmission by inhalation of aerosolized virus particles
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Low infectious dose required for infection. The human Calicivirus, better known as Norwalk virus, is an important cause of viral gastroenteritis, tends to occur in outbreak fashion, and can cause infection with as few as 10 virus particles. Caliciviruses are nonenveloped viruses and are thus more resistant to environmental conditions than enveloped viruses. Caliciviruses are resistant to desiccation and to chlorine levels as high as 10 ppm — making environmental decontamination difficult. Immunity is short-lived and there is no vaccine. Outbreaks are associated most commonly with contaminated food. Person-to-person transmission via fecal–oral route or contaminated fomites also leads to outbreaks. The virus can become aerosolized from fecal material or vomitus, and infection can occur following such exposure, but this route is not common.
keypoints: ⭐ Norovirus (Calicivirus) requires as few as 10 particles to cause infection — one of the lowest infectious doses of any pathogen
⭐ Nonenveloped viruses (Norovirus, HAV, Poliovirus) resist chlorine, detergents, and desiccation — highly stable in the environment
⭐ Immunity to Norovirus is short-lived and strain-specific; no vaccine available — explains repeated outbreaks in closed settings
Primary route: fecal–oral via contaminated food (shellfish, salads); aerosolized vomitus is a secondary route; classic outbreak settings: cruise ships, nursing homes, schools

questions.stem: A number of antivirals are termed nucleoside analogs. Which one of the following best describes the mode of action of nucleoside analogs?
choices: Insert within the helix of DNA to prevent viral replication
Bind to ribosomes and prevent anticodon–codon interactions thereby inhibiting protein synthesis
Substitute for nucleosides resulting in replication termination (chain termination)
Bind directly to DNA polymerase binding sites on viral genome to prevent viral replication
Bind directly to RNA polymerase binding sites on viral genome to prevent expression of viral gene products
questions.explanation: The answer is C: Substitute for nucleosides resulting in replication termination (chain termination). Nucleoside analogs are structures that mimic natural nucleosides used in the elongation of DNA during replication. These analogs have altered structures at points where phosphodiester bonds are to form between nucleosides in the growing DNA chain. Without the proper structure, chain elongation is terminated. Nucleoside analogs do not insert into the DNA helix (those are called intercalating agents). Some antimicrobial agents such as tetracycline bind to ribosomes and prevent protein synthesis, but this is not the mechanism of nucleoside analogs. There is no binding of nucleoside analogs to DNA or RNA polymerase recognition sites in the viral genome.
keypoints: ⭐ Nucleoside analogs (acyclovir, zidovudine, lamivudine, tenofovir) act as chain terminators — they lack the 3'-OH group needed to extend the DNA chain
⭐ Key requirement: most nucleoside analogs must be phosphorylated (activated) by viral or cellular kinases before they are incorporated into the growing chain
⭐ Acyclovir is selectively phosphorylated by HSV thymidine kinase → incorporated by viral DNA polymerase → chain termination; minimal toxicity to host cells
Distinguish: nucleoside analogs (chain termination) vs. non-nucleoside RT inhibitors (allosteric binding to polymerase) vs. protease inhibitors (block polyprotein cleavage)

questions.stem: A 56-year-old Southeast Asian immigrant is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B virus infection. Considering the epidemiology of this infection in endemic countries, what is the most likely way that this man became infected?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Perinatally. In developing countries — particularly Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Indian subcontinent — HBV is endemic and most commonly transmitted from a chronically infected mother to her newborn during birth. The infant is exposed to virus present in vaginal secretions and blood. HBV does not cross the placenta. Infection of newborns most commonly leads to chronic infection, whereas infection of adults (as occurs in nonendemic countries) most commonly leads to acute self-limited infection. Prevention includes administration of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIg) and the active recombinant vaccine at birth. The other mechanisms of transmission (sexual, IV drug use, needlestick) occur more commonly in developed countries where HBV is not endemic and infection occurs in adults.
keypoints: ⭐ In endemic regions (SE Asia, sub-Saharan Africa), perinatal transmission (mother → neonate) is the dominant route → leads to chronic HBV in >90% of cases
⭐ Key principle: age at infection determines chronicity — neonates >90% chronic; young children ~30%; adults <5% chronic
⭐ HBV does not cross the placenta; transmission occurs at delivery (vaginal secretions, blood) or post-natally (breast milk rare)
Prevention: HBIg + recombinant HBV vaccine at birth for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers — highly effective (>95%)

questions.stem: A medication used for this patient acts by inhibiting reverse transcriptase. Which antiviral medication, used for chronic HBV infections, works by inhibiting this enzyme?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Lamivudine. The replication cycle of HBV includes the viral enzyme reverse transcriptase; thus, inhibitors of this enzyme are therapeutic agents. Currently approved drugs that inhibit HBV reverse transcriptase include lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, and telbivudine. None of the other antivirals listed are used for HBV: acyclovir is used to treat HSV or VZV infections; fomivirsen and ganciclovir are used to treat CMV infections; and amprenavir is a protease inhibitor used to treat HIV.
keypoints: ⭐ HBV uses reverse transcriptase to replicate — its DNA genome is made via an RNA intermediate, making it susceptible to RT inhibitors
⭐ HBV reverse transcriptase inhibitors: lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, telbivudine, tenofovir — all nucleoside/nucleotide analogs
⭐ Entecavir and tenofovir are first-line due to high potency and low resistance rates; lamivudine has high resistance rates with prolonged use
Pegylated IFN-α is the other major HBV treatment (immune-mediated HCC reduction + finite course); combined with RT inhibitors in some regimens

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman presented with an insidious onset of fever, fatigue, joint pain, nausea, anorexia, and abdominal pain. Physical exam revealed hepatomegaly. A hepatitis panel revealed: HBsAg-positive, Anti-HBsAg-negative, Anti-HBcAg IgM-positive, HBeAg-positive, Anti-HAV IgG-positive. What is a correct interpretation of the hepatitis panel?
questions.explanation: The answer is A: Acute infection with HBV. The finding of surface antigen (HBsAg) combined with IgM antibodies to the core antigen (anti-HBcAg IgM) is consistent with acute HBV infection. Antibodies to the surface antigen are not found in the presence of detectable surface antigen. The 'e' antigen (HBeAg) indicates active viral replication and may or may not be detected in acute infections. The presence of IgG to HAV indicates either a past HAV infection or prior vaccination against HAV — not a coinfection with active HAV. Vaccination against HBV produces only anti-HBsAg antibodies (no core antibody); chronic infection produces IgG (total) anti-HBcAg; recovery produces both anti-HBsAg and anti-HBcAg IgG.
keypoints: ⭐ Acute HBV = HBsAg+ + anti-HBcAg IgM+ (IgM is the key marker of acute infection); anti-HBsAg absent when HBsAg present
⭐ HBeAg = active viral replication and high infectivity; its clearance and appearance of anti-HBeAg = 'e' seroconversion
⭐ Window period: HBsAg cleared but anti-HBsAg not yet detectable — only anti-HBcAg IgM is positive
Anti-HAV IgG = past HAV infection OR vaccination; it has no bearing on current HBV status

questions.stem: Considering the epidemiology of HBV infection in the United States, what would the history of the above patient (with acute HBV) most likely include?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Unprotected sex with multiple partners. Sexual activity is the most common mode of transmission of HBV in the United States. Intravenous drug abuse, while another important mode of transmission, is less common than sexual activity. Donated blood is screened for the presence of HBV, HCV, and other bloodborne pathogens; thus, transfusion-associated infections are rare in the United States. While alcoholism and cocaine addiction can lead to risky sexual behavior, they are not independent risk factors for HBV transmission.
keypoints: ⭐ In the United States (non-endemic), sexual transmission is the most common route of HBV — contrast with endemic countries where perinatal transmission dominates
⭐ IV drug abuse is second most common in the US; blood transfusion risk is now very low due to universal screening
⭐ HBV is 50–100× more infectious than HIV; transmitted via blood, sexual contact, and perinatally
HBV vaccination is recommended for all infants, unvaccinated children/adolescents, healthcare workers, and high-risk adults

questions.stem: The patient with acute HBV is seen 2 years later for treatment of gonorrhea. Liver function tests reveal elevated alanine transferase levels. A follow-up hepatitis panel revealed: HBsAg-positive, Anti-HBsAg-negative, Anti-HBcAg IgM-negative, Total anti-HBcAg-positive, HBeAg-positive, Anti-HBeAg-negative, Anti-HAV IgG-positive. What is a correct interpretation of the hepatitis panel?
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Chronic infection with HBV. The finding of surface antigen (HBsAg) in the serum for over 6 months is indicative of chronic HBV infection. By this time, IgM antibodies to the core antigen would be replaced with IgG antibodies (referred to as total anti-HBcAg). The presence of HBeAg is indicative of a greater degree of virus replication and higher transmissibility, though it may or may not be present in all chronic infections. The presence of IgG to HAV indicates a past infection or vaccination — unrelated to the current HBV status. Recovery from HBV would require anti-HBsAg antibodies, which are absent here.
keypoints: ⭐ Chronic HBV = HBsAg persisting >6 months + total anti-HBcAg (IgG) + NO anti-HBsAg; IgM anti-HBcAg is absent (replaced by IgG)
⭐ HBeAg+ in chronic HBV = high replication phase ('e' antigen positive = highly infectious); seroconversion to anti-HBeAg = lower viral load
⭐ Summary mnemonic — 4 HBV states: Acute (IgM core+, surface+), Chronic (total IgG core+, surface+, no surface Ab), Recovery (surface Ab + core IgG), Vaccinated (surface Ab ONLY, no core Ab)
Complications of chronic HBV: cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma; HBsAg+ patients should be monitored with AFP and liver ultrasound every 6 months

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents to his family physician in a small Georgia town with an acute onset of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Hepatomegaly and icteric sclera are noted on physical exam. Alanine transferase and aspartate transferase levels are markedly elevated. Over the next 3 days, 10 more people in the town seek medical attention with similar complaints. How is the most likely cause of this outbreak definitively diagnosed?
choices: Culture of organism on MacConkey agar
Demonstration of IgM antibodies against the agent
questions.explanation: The answer is C: Demonstration of IgM antibodies against the agent. The case describes an outbreak of infectious acute hepatitis. The most common infectious cause of acute hepatitis outbreaks in the United States is hepatitis A virus (HAV). This agent is diagnosed by the demonstration of IgM antiviral antibodies in the patient's serum. Although HAV is shed in the stool, most viral shedding occurs prior to the onset of symptoms, so stool detection is not useful diagnostically at this stage. HAV is also not isolated from blood. Bacteria and parasites are not commonly associated with acute hepatitis outbreaks in the United States.
keypoints: ⭐ HAV is the most common cause of acute hepatitis outbreaks in the United States; diagnosis = anti-HAV IgM (positive during acute illness)
⭐ HAV is transmitted fecal-orally (contaminated food/water); maximum viral shedding in stool occurs BEFORE symptom onset — explains rapid cluster outbreaks
⭐ Anti-HAV IgG (without IgM) = past infection or vaccination; HAV never causes chronic infection
HAV is an RNA picornavirus; no antiviral treatment exists; prevention via HAV vaccine (given at age 1 year + booster 6 months later)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman in apparent good health is found to have slightly elevated serum liver enzymes during an insurance physical. Follow-up investigations revealed antibodies to hepatitis C virus. What test could be done to distinguish between current infection and previous infection with full recovery?
questions.explanation: The answer is C: Reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction. Although the finding of elevated serum liver enzymes in a patient with antibodies to hepatitis C virus (HCV) is sufficient to make a diagnosis of ongoing infection, demonstration of the virus by reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) confirms active viral replication. In addition, a quantitative RT-PCR should be done prior to treatment to assess viral load. Culture of HCV is not possible at this time due to a lack of susceptible cell lines. ELISA and western blot were most likely used to determine the positive serology — they detect antibodies that persist whether infection is active or resolved. Indirect fluorescent antibody tests are not used in the diagnosis of HCV infection.
keypoints: ⭐ Anti-HCV antibodies persist long after infection clears — they cannot distinguish active from resolved infection
⭐ RT-PCR for HCV RNA is the gold standard to confirm active viremia and measure viral load
⭐ Diagnostic algorithm: ELISA screening → confirmed by RT-PCR (or RIBA); quantitative RT-PCR before treatment for baseline viral load
HCV has no cell culture system; ~15–25% of acutely infected individuals spontaneously clear the virus; the rest develop chronic infection

questions.stem: Three years following diagnosis with hepatitis C virus, liver biopsy from the above patient reveals sufficient damage to consider antiviral therapy. With which drug combination should she be treated?
questions.explanation: The answer is D: Pegylated interferon and ribavirin. This combination of drugs is the standard therapy for HCV-infected patients regardless of genotype. Patients with genotypes 2 or 3 are treated for 24 weeks whereas those with genotype 1 are treated for 48 weeks. Adefovir and lamivudine are used for hepatitis B virus. Lamivudine plus zidovudine are nucleoside RT inhibitors used for HIV. Amoxicillin plus sulbactam and TMP-SMZ are antibacterial combinations with no activity against HCV.
keypoints: ⭐ Classic HCV treatment: pegylated interferon-α + ribavirin — duration depends on genotype (genotype 1 = 48 wks, genotypes 2/3 = 24 wks)
⭐ Ribavirin mechanism: inhibits synthesis of GTP (guanosine triphosphate), reducing the nucleotide pool needed for viral RNA replication
⭐ Genotype 1 (most common in US) responds poorly to interferon/ribavirin (~50% SVR); genotypes 2/3 respond better (~80% SVR)
Modern context: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs — NS5B inhibitors, NS3/4A protease inhibitors, NS5A inhibitors) have largely replaced interferon/ribavirin with >95% cure rates

questions.stem: A fourth year medical student sustains a needlestick from a patient being evaluated for jaundice. A hepatitis panel is ordered on the student the same day and finds: HBsAg-negative, Anti-HBsAg-positive, Anti-HBcAg IgM-negative, Anti-HBcAg total negative, Anti-HAV IgG-positive, Anti-HCV-negative. What is a correct interpretation of the hepatitis panel?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Vaccinated against HBV and HAV. Vaccines are available for both hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV), and vaccination of healthcare workers against HBV is required or strongly recommended. Vaccination against HBV results in antibodies to the surface antigen (anti-HBsAg) ONLY — no core antibody (anti-HBcAg) is produced because the recombinant vaccine contains only the surface antigen protein. Conversely, natural infection produces core antibodies (IgM initially, then IgG total). Acute infection would show anti-HBcAg IgM; chronic infection would show total anti-HBcAg (IgG). Past infection with HBV would show both anti-HBsAg AND anti-HBcAg (IgG). The presence of anti-HAV IgG indicates vaccination or prior HAV infection. The student is protected from both viruses.
keypoints: ⭐ HBV vaccination → anti-HBsAg ONLY (no anti-HBcAg) — the recombinant vaccine contains only HBsAg protein
⭐ Natural HBV infection (recovery) → anti-HBsAg + anti-HBcAg IgG — core antibody distinguishes natural immunity from vaccine immunity
⭐ Summary: anti-HBsAg alone = vaccinated; anti-HBsAg + anti-HBcAg IgG = recovered; HBsAg + anti-HBcAg IgM = acute; HBsAg + anti-HBcAg IgG (total) = chronic
Healthcare workers should be tested for anti-HBsAg after completing the 3-dose vaccine series; non-responders (~5%) may need revaccination

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male is diagnosed with acute hepatitis due to hepatitis C virus. Based on the epidemiology of this infection in the United States, how did this man most likely become infected?
questions.explanation: The answer is A: Intravenous drug abuse. Epidemiological surveys of acute hepatitis indicate that intravenous drug abuse is the most common mode of transmission of hepatitis C virus (HCV) in the United States. Of newly diagnosed cases, approximately 54% were attributed to intravenous drug use. Sexual transmission is possible, particularly among persons engaging in unprotected sex with multiple partners; however, persons in monogamous sexual relationships do not appear to be at increased risk when one partner is infected. Needlestick injury is an uncommon route. Transfusion-associated infections are now rare since the development of sensitive tests to screen donated blood.
keypoints: ⭐ IV drug abuse is the #1 mode of HCV transmission in the United States (~54% of new cases)
⭐ Sexual transmission is possible with multiple partners but very low risk in monogamous relationships — contrasts with HBV (easily sexually transmitted)
⭐ Blood transfusion was the leading cause pre-1992 (before HCV screening); now very rare (<1:2 million units transfused)
HCV = major cause of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide; no vaccine available; DAAs now provide >95% cure
